title: Profile first: measure where time actually goes, not where you think it goes
summary: Why guessing wrong is the default when you optimise without data, how Amdahl's law caps every speedup you can ever ship, and the measurement loop senior engineers run before touching a line of code.
crux: Optimise without profiling = guess. Empirically, the guess is wrong more than half the time. Profile first or pay for it in churn.
keytakeaway: Profile-first is the chapter's foundation. Amdahl bounds your speedup; the profile names the function. Without measurement, optimisation is guessing — empirically wrong over half the time.

title: Hot paths: read the hotspot, attack the right axis, verify the diff
summary: Once the profile names the hot function, how to classify what's actually expensive (CPU vs alloc vs cache vs lock vs syscall), the categorical fix that maps to each shape, and the diff that proves the fix landed.
crux: Wide frame = hot. But hot from what? CPU, alloc, cache, lock, syscall — different shapes, different fixes. Diagnose first.
keytakeaway: Wide leaf names the symptom; diagnose the category (CPU, alloc, cache, lock, syscall, JIT deopt) before the fix. Category picks the toolbox; the diff proves the fix landed.

title: Cache vs big-O: when the textbook lies about your real performance
summary: Why an O(N) loop can beat an O(log N) one, how cache lines and branch prediction dominate modern CPU performance, and the data-layout choices that make algorithms 10-50x faster without changing the algorithm.
crux: Big-O is asymptotic. Cache locality is real. Same O(N²): row-major loop 300ms, column-major 2800ms — same algorithm, 9x slower.
keytakeaway: Big-O is asymptotic. Cache and branch behaviour are the real wall-clock truth. Same algorithm, different layout = 10-50x speed difference.

title: Garbage collection: pause budgets, allocation pressure, and the tail you don't see
summary: How modern GCs trade pause time, throughput, and memory; why generational and concurrent algorithms exist; and how allocation pressure in your code becomes p99 latency in your service.
crux: GC reclaims unreachable memory. Pause time, throughput, and heap size are a 3-way tradeoff. Allocation pressure is what you control.
keytakeaway: GC pause = symptom; allocation pressure = cause. Reduce allocations first, tune the collector second, switch collectors last. Three-way tradeoff: pause, throughput, heap.

title: N+1: one logical operation, many round-trips
summary: Why one screen renders into 200 database queries, the four fix patterns (JOIN, IN, batch-loader, prefetch) with their tradeoffs, and how the same problem repeats across REST, gRPC, and microservice fan-out.
crux: One trip = fast. N+1 trips = slow. Each round-trip pays RTT; one query of 100 rows beats 100 queries of one row.
keytakeaway: N+1 = many small round-trips dominating wall-clock. Diagnose with query log or APM, not CPU profile. Fix family: JOIN / IN / preload / DataLoader. Verify by query count drop.

title: Batching: amortise the fixed cost of every operation
summary: When a per-operation cost is mostly fixed (syscall, network round-trip, ACK), grouping operations into batches amortises that cost; the size/time window decides where throughput meets tail-latency.
crux: Per-op fixed cost dominates? Batch. Window = batch size and max wait; bigger batches buy throughput, charge tail-latency.
keytakeaway: Batching amortises a fixed cost across N operations. Window = max-size + max-wait. Bigger batches buy throughput, cost tail-latency. Tune to SLO ceiling, not max throughput.

title: Bundle budgets: the bytes your users actually pay for
summary: Why JavaScript bundle size dominates client-side performance, how to set per-route budgets the team can enforce, and the levers (split, tree-shake, defer, compress, preload) that keep mid-range mobile fast.
crux: JS bundle bytes = parse + compile + execute on user's CPU. Mid-range mobile = 4-8x slower than dev laptop. Set a budget, enforce it.
keytakeaway: Bundle bytes = parse + compile + execute on user CPU. Set per-route budgets, enforce at CI, monitor with RUM. Smaller bundle = faster LCP, better INP, no architecture change.
